title: Contexts of production and reception
summary: Every text is shaped by when, where and why it was made, and read differently in different times and places. Learn to use context to sharpen analysis, not replace it.

keyterms.definition: The circumstances surrounding a text, including historical, social, cultural, political and personal factors.
The circumstances in which a text was created: its time, place, culture, medium and the writer's situation.
The circumstances in which a text is read or viewed, which can change its meaning over time.
Events, values and conditions of the period in which a text was made or is set.
The channel through which a text reaches its audience, e.g. print, radio, film, social media.
Something placed in a time where it does not belong, sometimes used deliberately for effect.
The dominant spirit, mood or set of ideas of a particular period.
The body of works traditionally regarded as the most important in a literature; its membership is contested.
The suppression or control of texts or speech, which can shape what writers say and how indirectly they say it.
Reclaiming a word, image or text by a group and giving it new meaning, often in a new context.

questions.prompt: A wartime poster urges: "Waste not, want not: every crust counts." Which context best explains its message?
questions.explanation: Thrift messages make sense in a context of scarcity; context explains why the appeal would resonate.

questions.text: The circumstances in which a text is read, rather than written, are its context of ___.
questions.explanation: Reception context changes as audiences, values and media change.

questions.statement: In Paper 1, long paragraphs of historical background earn credit even if they are not linked to the text's features.
questions.explanation: Context should illuminate specific choices in the text; unlinked background is padding.

questions.prompt: A 1950s advert shows a smiling housewife thrilled by a new vacuum cleaner. How might a reader today respond differently from its original audience?
options: By noticing and questioning its gender stereotypes
By assuming it is a parody of a modern advert
questions.explanation: Shifting values in the context of reception lead modern readers to see stereotypes that the original audience may have taken for granted.

questions.prompt: Match the medium to a typical feature it allows.

pairs.right: Sound effects and tone of voice

questions.explanation: The medium shapes what a text can do; analysis should consider its affordances.

questions.prompt: A writer living under a strict regime tells a fable about a lion who silences other animals. Why might she choose allegory?
options: To criticise power indirectly and avoid censorship
To write for very young children only
questions.explanation: Indirect forms like allegory allow critique where direct criticism would be dangerous.

questions.text: The channel through which a text reaches its audience, such as print or podcast, is its ___.
questions.explanation: Medium and genre differ: an opinion piece (genre) can appear in print or online (medium).

questions.statement: The same speech can gain new meanings when it is quoted decades later in a different struggle.
questions.explanation: Reception changes meaning: words are re-read through the concerns of new audiences.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses context most effectively in analysis?
options: The war ended in 1918, which was a very important event.
Written months after the war, the poem's broken lines echo a generation's shattered certainty.
The poet was born in a small town.
questions.explanation: Effective use links context directly to a textual feature and its effect.

questions.prompt: Order these media by when they first became mass media, earliest first.
questions.explanation: Each new medium changed how texts reach audiences and how audiences talk back.

options: A fixed list approved by the IB
A contested body of works traditionally seen as most important
Any book sold in an airport
questions.explanation: The canon is shaped by power and taste and has been challenged for excluding many voices.

questions.statement: Debates about the canon are relevant to this course, which asks students to study works from different places, periods and translations.
questions.explanation: The course encourages a range of works and critical thinking about whose writing counts as literature.

questions.text: The dominant spirit or mood of a period is its ___.
questions.explanation: Texts often capture or react against the zeitgeist of their time.

questions.prompt: A community reclaims a slur once used against it and uses it with pride in song lyrics. What is this?
questions.explanation: Reappropriation transforms meaning by changing who uses a word and in what context.

questions.prompt: A modern film of a classic play has characters texting on smartphones. What is this choice?
options: A deliberate anachronism to make the story feel contemporary
questions.explanation: Deliberate anachronism bridges contexts and suggests the story's concerns are timeless.

questions.prompt: Match the context type to an example.

pairs.right: The writer recently lost a parent

questions.explanation: Naming the precise kind of context makes analysis sharper.

questions.statement: A text's meaning is fixed at the moment it is written and never changes.
questions.explanation: Meaning shifts with readers and contexts of reception; this is central to the time and space area of exploration.

questions.prompt: A 1970s magazine article confidently predicts flying cars by 2000. How does reading it now affect its tone?
questions.explanation: Hindsight in the context of reception can make earnest texts seem ironic or naïve.

questions.text: The suppression or control of texts by authorities is called ___.
questions.explanation: Censorship shapes both what is published and how writers encode meaning.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to know that a speech was first broadcast on radio?
options: It explains the reliance on sound, rhythm and repetition rather than visuals
It tells us the speaker's age
It proves the speech was fictional
It is not useful at all
questions.explanation: Medium is part of the context of production and shapes technique: radio rewards memorable sound patterns.
